newsitem.title: USA: Michigan prosecutor says will not re-try Kevorkian.
newsitem.headline: Michigan prosecutor says will not re-try Kevorkian.

text.p: The Ionia County prosecutor said Friday he will not re-try Dr. Jack Kevorkian on charges of assisted suicide and practicing medicine without a license because chances of success were minimal.

A mistrial was declared June 12 in the west-central Michigan case involving the death of 54-year-old Loretta Peabody, who suffered from multiple sclerosis. Kevorkian had been accused of helping Peabody die in August 1996 with a lethal injection.

The case ended on its second day of arguments when Ionia County Circuit Judge Charles Miel granted prosecutor Raymond Voet's request for a mistrial because of improper opening statements from defence attorney Geoffrey Fieger.

In an 11-page statement, Voet said he could not justify using the county's resources to try another case. His reasons included a lack of cooperation from Peabody's family members and the likelihood that Kevorkian would not receive a meaningful sentence.
Voet also said he was also concerned about the judicial system's ability to control Feiger.

"Until the legal profession finds a backbone, the unfortunate truth is that Fieger will continue to be successful by flouting the rules of conduct and civility that make our legal system work," Voet said in a statement.
A spokeswoman for Fieger said he was in court and not available for comment.
Kevorkian has been acquitted at three previous assisted suicide trials involving five deaths. The 69-year-old retired pathologist has admitted being present at 45 deaths since 1990.
Since February, Fieger has hinted Kevorkian was involved in two others, and eight more bodies have been found with notes referring authorities to Fieger.
